html:
The Seleucid Empire was a Greek kingdom in West Asia founded by Seleucus I, one of Alexander's generals, in 312 BCE, and ended by Rome in 63 BCE. At its height it stretched from the Aegean to the borders of India and held most of the Asian lands taken in Alexander's conquests.

After Alexander died, his generals fought over his empire for decades. Seleucus took Babylon in 312 BCE, and then won Iran and the east. He gave up the lands along the Indus to Chandragupta Maurya in return for five hundred war elephants, which helped him win the battles that followed.

The Seleucids ruled from Seleucia on the Tigris and later Antioch in Syria. They founded many Greek cities, which spread Greek language and culture across the region, alongside older Babylonian, Persian and Jewish traditions. They fought a long series of wars with Ptolemaic Egypt over Syria and Palestine.

Its story is one of slow shrinking:

  • Bactria, in today's Afghanistan, broke away around 250 BCE.
  • The Parthians took Iran and then Mesopotamia, by about 140 BCE.
  • Antiochus III won back much of the east but was beaten by Rome in 190 BCE and had to give up Anatolia.
  • His son Antiochus IV tried to force Greek religion on Judea, which set off the Maccabean revolt in 167 BCE and led to an independent Jewish state.

By the first century BCE the empire was little more than Syria, torn by fights within the royal family. In 63 BCE the Roman general Pompey made it a Roman province.
